# Connecting C++ and QML {#sec-cpp-qml}

C++ holds the state, QML shows it (@sec-split). Between them is one contract: a C++ object
offers properties, signals and invokable methods (@sec-properties), and QML binds to them
and calls them. This chapter shows how your C++ types become QML types, how your objects get
into QML, what crosses the boundary as a plain value, and when to draw with C++ yourself.

## QML modules and declarative registration {#sec-qml-modules}

Mark a C++ class `QML_ELEMENT`, list it in a QML module, and QML can use it under the
module's name. There is no registration code in `main()`.

```{.cpp filename="CanvasStore.hpp"}
#include <QtCore/QObject>
#include <QtQmlIntegration/qqmlintegration.h>

class CanvasStore : public QObject
{
    Q_OBJECT
    QML_ELEMENT
    // properties, methods, signals
};
```

```{.cmake filename="src/canvas/CMakeLists.txt"}
qt_add_qml_module(app_canvas
    URI App.Canvas
    STATIC
    SOURCES CanvasStore.cpp CanvasStore.hpp
    QML_FILES CanvasPage.qml
)
```

```qml
import App.Canvas   // CanvasStore and CanvasPage are now types
```

From this one call, the build generates the whole QML module, including a type description
for the QML tools. The tools learn every type, property and method of the module, which is
what makes typed QML (@sec-typed-qml) possible.

`STATIC` builds the module into the executable instead of a plugin that Qt loads at run
time. The app then ships with its QML inside, and nothing can go missing on the user's
machine. For the modules of one application, that is the simpler choice.

::: {.callout-warning}
## Static modules need their plugin
The linker drops code from a static library that nothing calls, and nothing calls the
registration. Link the plugin target, `app_canvasplugin`, not just `app_canvas`, into the
executable and into QML tests; it makes sure the module registers itself.
:::

::: {.more}
**Template:** `src/canvas/CMakeLists.txt`

**Read more:** [Defining QML types from C++](https://doc.qt.io/qt-6/qtqml-cppintegration-definetypes.html)
:::

## Enums across the boundary {#sec-qml-enums}

QML can use a C++ enum as a property or method argument when its enclosing type has Qt
metadata. The canvas declares `PaperBackground` in a namespace marked `Q_NAMESPACE`,
registers it with `Q_ENUM_NS`, and exposes the namespace to QML as `Paper` with
`QML_NAMED_ELEMENT`. List the header in the QML module so the build generates its metadata.
The store then exposes the enum itself, and QML uses values such as `Paper.Dots` rather
than unexplained integers.

```qml
store.setPaperBackground(Paper.Dots)
```

For a type owned by another library, use `QML_FOREIGN` or `QML_FOREIGN_NAMESPACE` in an
integration header instead of changing the library. The foreign type or namespace must
already have Qt meta-object information and registered enums; the foreign macro does not
create that metadata. If it has none, add a Qt-facing wrapper and explicitly map its
values at the boundary.

::: {.more}
**Template:** `src/canvas/Sketch.hpp`, `src/canvas/CanvasStore.hpp`

**Read more:** [QML enumerations](https://doc.qt.io/qt-6/qtqml-typesystem-enumerations.html),
[foreign QML types](https://doc.qt.io/qt-6/qqmlintegration-h.html)
:::

## Passing objects in {#sec-required}

How an object gets into QML depends on who creates it. The important objects of an
application (its view models, stores and services) are created by `main()`, which also
connects them to each other (@sec-composition-root). QML receives them. The main QML file
declares what it needs, and `main()` provides it before loading the file:

```{.qml filename="Main.qml"}
ApplicationWindow {
    id: window
    required property SketchbookViewModel sketchbook
    required property CanvasStore canvas

    CanvasPage { store: window.canvas }   // pages get their objects the same way
}
```

```{.cpp filename="main.cpp"}
engine.setInitialProperties({
    { "sketchbook", QVariant::fromValue(&sketchbook) },
    { "canvas", QVariant::fromValue(&canvas) },
});
engine.loadFromModule("App", "Main");
```

Every page states what it depends on, with a type the tools can check. A test can load any
page on its own and give it whatever objects the test needs.

Mark such classes `QML_UNCREATABLE("Created in main()")`, so QML cannot create a second,
unconnected instance by mistake. They are still QML types: QML can use them in property
declarations and read their enums.

::: {.callout-warning}
## Never use context properties
`rootContext()->setContextProperty("canvas", &canvas)` injects a name that no tool can see
or type-check. It is the Qt 5 way. Required properties replace it.
:::

::: {.more}
**Template:** `src/app/main.cpp`, `src/app/Main.qml`

**Read more:** [Exposing C++ state to QML](https://doc.qt.io/qt-6/qtqml-cppintegration-exposecppstate.html)
:::

## Singletons for app-wide state {#sec-singletons}

Some state is needed by every view: the language, the build information. Passing it through
every component would be noise. Make it a QML singleton, but create the instance yourself:

```{.cpp filename="AppController.hpp"}
class AppController : public QObject
{
    Q_OBJECT
    QML_ELEMENT
    QML_SINGLETON
    QML_UNCREATABLE("Created in main()")
    Q_PROPERTY(QString language READ language WRITE setLanguage
               NOTIFY languageChanged FINAL)
    // ...
};
```

```{.cpp filename="main.cpp"}
AppController controller(logFile);
engine.setExternalSingletonInstance("App", "AppController", &controller);
```

```qml
onClicked: AppController.language = "de"
```

`setExternalSingletonInstance()`, new in Qt 6.12, lets `main()` construct the singleton
with its real dependencies, like any other object, and lets a test construct its own. Keep
singletons rare: most objects belong to a feature and arrive as required properties.

::: {.more}
**Template:** `src/app/AppController.hpp`
:::

## Objects that belong to one view {#sec-qml-types}

Leave out `QML_UNCREATABLE`, and QML can create the type itself, like a `Timer`:

```qml
Stopwatch {
    id: watch
    running: recordButton.checked
}
```

The object lives as long as the QML object that declares it, and every page that declares
one gets its own. That suits helpers that belong to a single view and need C++, such as a
parser or a wrapper around a platform API. As soon as several views share an object, or it
has to outlive a page, create it in `main()` and pass it in instead.

::: {.more}
**Read more:** [Defining QML types from C++](https://doc.qt.io/qt-6/qtqml-cppintegration-definetypes.html)
:::

## Values cross as copies {#sec-value-types}

Only `QObject`s cross the boundary by reference. Everything else is copied: numbers,
strings, colors, points, and lists of them, such as the `QList<QPointF>` of a stroke. A
copy has no identity and no signals, so QML cannot watch it change. When a value changes,
the property that holds it notifies, and QML reads the new copy.

Collections the user sees do not belong in such a list. Give them a model instead
(@sec-item-models), so a view can update one row at a time.

Enums come from `Q_ENUM` inside a registered class, and QML reads them by the class name:

```{.cpp filename="CanvasStore.hpp"}
enum class Shape : quint8 { Circle, Rectangle, Triangle };
Q_ENUM(Shape)
Q_SIGNAL void shapeSnapped(app::canvas::CanvasStore::Shape shape);
```

```qml
function onShapeSnapped(shape: int): void {
    if (shape === CanvasStore.Shape.Circle)
        hint.text = qsTr("Snapped to a circle");
}
```

In QML an enum value is a number, and an enum is not a type: annotate the parameter as
`int`, or qmllint reports it.

For a small struct of your own, register a value type: a `Q_GADGET` with
`QML_VALUE_TYPE` and a name that starts with a lower-case letter, such as `sample`.

::: {.more}
**Template:** `src/canvas/CanvasStore.hpp`, and the snap hint in `src/canvas/CanvasPage.qml`

**Read more:** [Data type conversion between QML and C++](https://doc.qt.io/qt-6/qtqml-cppintegration-data.html)
:::

## Item models in C++ {#sec-item-models}

Collections reach QML as item models. Subclass `QAbstractListModel`, name your roles, and
report every change as precisely as you can:

```{.cpp filename="SketchListModel.cpp"}
int SketchListModel::rowCount(const QModelIndex &parent) const
{
    return parent.isValid() ? 0 : static_cast<int>(m_entries.size());
}

QVariant SketchListModel::data(const QModelIndex &index, int role) const
{
    if (!checkIndex(index, CheckIndexOption::IndexIsValid))
        return {};
    const auto &entry = m_entries.at(index.row());
    switch (role) {
    case NameRole: return entry.name;
    case StrokeCountRole: return entry.strokeCount;
    default: return {};
    }
}

QHash<int, QByteArray> SketchListModel::roleNames() const
{
    return { { NameRole, "name" }, { StrokeCountRole, "strokeCount" } };  // <1>
}

void SketchListModel::prepend(SketchEntry entry)
{
    beginInsertRows({}, 0, 0);  // <2>
    m_entries.insert(m_entries.begin(), std::move(entry));
    endInsertRows();
}
```
1. The role names become the delegate's required properties (@sec-lists).
2. "One row arrives at the top": the view adds one delegate and keeps its scroll position.

Prefer `beginInsertRows`, `beginRemoveRows` and `dataChanged` over a model reset. A reset
tells the view to throw everything away, so it loses scroll position, selection and any
running animation.

::: {.more}
**Template:** `src/sketchbook/SketchListModel.cpp`

**Read more:** [Model/view programming](https://doc.qt.io/qt-6/model-view-programming.html)
:::

## Custom visual items {#sec-custom-items}

Sometimes no built-in item can draw what you need: a waveform with thousands of samples, a
live chart, a drawing canvas. Then write the item in C++. It is a `QQuickItem` subclass
with `QML_ELEMENT`, so QML creates, positions and binds it like a `Rectangle`. Pick the
simplest option that is fast enough:

| Option | How it draws | Use it for |
|---|---|---|
| Qt Quick Shapes | vector paths declared in QML | icons and diagrams |
| `QQuickPaintedItem` | `QPainter` into an image, uploaded as a texture | simple drawing that rarely changes |
| Scene graph item | geometry nodes on the GPU | content that changes often, such as strokes or charts |
| `QQuickRhiItem` | your own rendering code and shaders, on every graphics API Qt supports | 3D and custom rendering |

A scene graph item sets `ItemHasContents` and builds its geometry in `updatePaintNode()`:

```{.cpp filename="LineItem.cpp"}
LineItem::LineItem(QQuickItem *parent)
    : QQuickItem(parent)
{
    setFlag(ItemHasContents);
}

QSGNode *LineItem::updatePaintNode(QSGNode *oldNode, UpdatePaintNodeData *)
{
    auto *node = static_cast<QSGGeometryNode *>(oldNode);
    if (!node) {                                                          // <1>
        node = new QSGGeometryNode;
        auto *geometry =
            new QSGGeometry(QSGGeometry::defaultAttributes_Point2D(), 0);
        geometry->setDrawingMode(QSGGeometry::DrawLineStrip);
        node->setGeometry(geometry);
        node->setFlag(QSGNode::OwnsGeometry);
        auto *material = new QSGFlatColorMaterial;
        material->setColor(Qt::black);
        node->setMaterial(material);
        node->setFlag(QSGNode::OwnsMaterial);
    }
    auto *geometry = node->geometry();                                    // <2>
    geometry->allocate(static_cast<int>(m_points.size()));
    auto *vertices = geometry->vertexDataAsPoint2D();
    for (qsizetype i = 0; i < m_points.size(); ++i)
        vertices[i].set(float(m_points[i].x()), float(m_points[i].y()));
    node->markDirty(QSGNode::DirtyGeometry);
    return node;
}
```
1. The first call creates the node; later calls receive it back and update it.
2. Only the vertices change on later calls. The node and its material stay.

To redraw, call `update()`, and Qt calls `updatePaintNode()` before the next frame. Reuse
nodes between frames and change only what changed. That is where a scene graph item beats a
painted item, which draws with `QPainter` on the CPU and uploads the image to the GPU after
every change.

::: {.callout-important}
## The render thread only builds nodes
`updatePaintNode()` runs on the render thread while the GUI thread waits. Reading the item's
data there is safe, because the GUI thread is paused. Changing the item, calling into QML or
touching any other QObject is not: that stays on the GUI thread.
:::

::: {.more}
**Template:** `src/canvas/StrokeItem.cpp`, which builds one node per stroke and keeps the
nodes of strokes that did not change

**Read more:** [The Qt Quick scene graph](https://doc.qt.io/qt-6/qtquick-visualcanvas-scenegraph.html)
:::

## Lifetimes across the boundary {#sec-lifetimes}

QML holds plain pointers to your C++ objects. Make sure those objects outlive the engine:
create them in `main()` before the engine, so C++ destroys them after it (@sec-composition-root).

One rule surprises almost everyone. Every `QObject *` that a `Q_INVOKABLE` method returns
**belongs to QML**. The garbage collector deletes it once no JavaScript uses it, unless it
has a parent.

```cpp
Q_INVOKABLE Document *createDocument();   // the result now belongs to QML
```

Give such objects a parent, or call
`QQmlEngine::setObjectOwnership(object, QQmlEngine::CppOwnership)` before returning them.
Objects that QML reads through a property stay owned by C++.

Calls go one way, too: C++ never reaches into QML. Looking up QML objects with
`findChild()` and calling their functions ties C++ to the structure of a view that changes
all the time, and no tool checks it. The Qt documentation recommends it only for tests.
Turn it around: C++ offers properties, signals and invokable methods, and QML uses them.

::: {.callout-important}
## Every object QML sees must outlive it
QML does not keep your C++ objects alive. If one is destroyed while QML still points to it,
the next binding reads freed memory. Create long-lived objects in `main()` before the engine,
and decide explicitly who owns every object you return to QML.
:::

::: {.more}
**Read more:** [Data ownership](https://doc.qt.io/qt-6/qtqml-cppintegration-data.html#data-ownership),
[Interacting with QML objects from C++](https://doc.qt.io/qt-6/qtqml-cppintegration-interactqmlfromcpp.html)
:::
